meta.title: NDIS / NDIC: Deposit Insurance and Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
meta.description: Comprehensive course on deposit insurance principles and the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) based on Access Bank ELTP 2025 materials.

questionBank.q: Which term describes an institutional guarantee that compensates savers, in whole or in part, if their bank becomes unable to repay them?
opts: Prudential regulation
Deposit insurance
Lender-of-last-resort support
Bank recapitalization
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance is the guarantee that protects depositors, particularly small savers, from losing their funds when a bank fails. Lender-of-last-resort support is attractive as a distractor because it is also part of the financial safety net, but it provides liquidity to solvent banks rather than compensating depositors directly. See 'What is Deposit Insurance?' in the manual.

questionBank.q: One stated reason a country adopts an explicit deposit insurance scheme is to formalize the shift away from which prior form of depositor protection?
opts: Privately arranged, fully collateralized insurance contracts
Implicit protection with no fixed rules
Central bank emergency lending to distressed banks
Shareholder-funded recapitalization arrangements for troubled banks
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance is often introduced specifically to formalize the transition from blanket or implicit protection to defined, limited coverage. Central bank lending is a distractor because it is a genuine safety-net function, but it is the lender-of-last-resort role, not a form of depositor protection being replaced. See 'Reasons for Deposit Insurance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which deposit insurance policy objective is specifically achieved by collecting premiums from every insured institution rather than billing only banks that actually fail?
opts: Guaranteeing unlimited payouts to every affected depositor
Spreading bank failure costs across all depositors
Shifting failure costs onto bank shareholders alone
Concentrating supervisory resources on distressed banks alone
questionBank.exp: Charging premiums to all insured banks, rather than only recovering costs from a failed bank after the fact, spreads the cost of failure system-wide. 'Concentrating supervisory costs on distressed banks' is attractive because failure resolution does focus scrutiny on troubled banks, but that is a supervisory practice, not the premium-funding objective being tested here. See 'DIS: Policy Objectives' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Besides deposit insurance, which two functions together make up the rest of a country's financial safety net?
opts: Deposit rate controls and mandatory bank mergers
Prudential supervision plus central bank lender-of-last-resort support
Foreign reserve accumulation and currency pegging
Capital market regulation and export financing schemes
questionBank.exp: The financial safety net has three pillars: deposit insurance, prudential regulation and supervision, and a central bank's lender-of-last-resort facility providing temporary liquidity to solvent banks. Currency pegging and reserve accumulation are real central bank activities, which makes that option tempting, but they are not classified as safety-net components in this framework. See 'Financial Safety Net' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor believes their ₦100 balance at the bank is exactly as usable and safe as ₦100 in their pocket. Which outcome does this belief represent?
opts: The bank has reached full liquidity coverage
Confidence in bank deposits has been achieved
The central bank has issued a blanket guarantee
The bank has passed its most recent examination
questionBank.exp: The manual defines confidence as being achieved precisely when a depositor sees bank deposits as equivalent to cash. A blanket guarantee is a plausible distractor because it is one systemic tool used to build confidence, but it is a specific policy action, not the confidence outcome itself. See 'Enhancing Public Confidence' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Even when a bank is fundamentally financially sound, what can still trigger a large-scale withdrawal of deposits that leads to its failure?
opts: A routine on-site examination
A loss of depositor confidence
An increase in the cash reserve requirement
A scheduled premium assessment
questionBank.exp: A bank run can occur purely from a loss of depositor confidence, independent of the bank's actual financial soundness -- which is exactly why deposit insurance exists to prevent it. A cash reserve requirement increase is a real regulatory tool and sounds plausible as a stressor, but it does not itself cause a run; confidence loss does. See 'A Run on a Bank' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What term describes the incentive for banks and depositors to take on excessive risk because deposit insurance shields them from the consequences?
opts: Adverse selection
Moral hazard
Systemic risk
Regulatory capture
questionBank.exp: Moral hazard is the incentive to take excessive risk created by the existence of a safety net. Adverse selection is a natural pairing distractor since it is the other classic DI design risk, but it concerns which institutions choose to participate, not risk-taking behavior after coverage exists. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer sets a cap on the amount it will reimburse any single depositor. Which problem is this design feature primarily intended to reduce?
opts: Adverse selection among participating banks
Moral hazard from excessive risk-taking
Delays in the failure resolution process
Duplication of supervisory examinations
questionBank.exp: Placing limits on the amounts insured is explicitly listed as a design feature that mitigates moral hazard, since large depositors retain an incentive to monitor bank risk when their full balance is not guaranteed. Adverse selection is tempting because it is the other major DI risk, but it is addressed through membership rules, not coverage limits. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: In a deposit insurance system where banks may choose whether to join, which type of institution is most likely to opt in?
opts: Lower-risk banks seeking premium discounts
Higher-risk banks seeking depositor protection
Foreign banks seeking regulatory exemptions
State-owned banks seeking capital injections
questionBank.exp: Adverse selection describes the tendency for higher-risk institutions to opt into voluntary deposit insurance while lower-risk ones opt out, which paradoxically raises the likelihood that a covered failure will occur. Lower-risk banks seeking discounts is a plausible-sounding distractor, but voluntary systems see the opposite pattern from safer banks. See 'DIS & Adverse Selection' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the four conditions necessary for deposit insurance to function effectively?
opts: A fixed exchange rate policy
A sound and effective legal regime
A single dominant state-owned bank
An unrestricted voluntary membership rule
questionBank.exp: Effective DI requires a sound legal regime, strong prudential regulation and supervision, sound accounting and financial reporting, and comprehensive bank disclosure. A fixed exchange rate policy is unrelated to DI's institutional preconditions, though it may sound like a plausible macroeconomic 'condition.' See 'Conditions for Effective DI' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A government arranges and financially supports the merger of a failing bank with a healthy one, preventing outright liquidation. Which type of deposit protection does this illustrate?
opts: Explicit deposit insurance
Implicit deposit insurance
Pass-through insurance
Differential premium assessment
questionBank.exp: This is a classic implicit deposit insurance action: an uncodified, discretionary government intervention rather than a pre-defined, legally established scheme. Explicit deposit insurance is the natural contrasting distractor, but explicit systems operate under codified rules, not case-by-case government arrangements. See 'Implicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a characteristic of an implicit deposit insurance scheme?
opts: A codified maximum insured amount set by statute
Uncertainty about the limit and scope of coverage
A dedicated fund built from member premiums
A published, fixed administration framework
questionBank.exp: Implicit schemes are unplanned and uncodified, so depositors face genuine uncertainty about how much protection they will actually receive and under what conditions. A codified maximum insured amount is instead a hallmark of explicit deposit insurance, which is exactly why it is an attractive but wrong choice here. See 'Characteristics of Implicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What is one advantage that a legally established, explicit deposit insurance scheme provides over an implicit one?
opts: A discretionary case-by-case decision process for each bank
Clear and efficient standards for resolving failed banks
A blanket guarantee extended to all creditors and shareholders
Direct government recapitalization rather than premium funding
questionBank.exp: Explicit systems specify rules and procedures in advance, giving clear, efficient standards for resolving failed banks -- one of their stated benefits over implicit, discretionary protection. A blanket guarantee to all creditors is tempting since 'guarantee' language overlaps, but blanket coverage is a distinct, temporary systemic tool, not a routine feature of explicit DIS. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Explicit deposit insurance mandates form a spectrum. Which pair correctly represents the two ends of that spectrum?
opts: Blanket protection and premium assessments
Pay-box systems and risk minimizers
Implicit schemes and pass-through insurance
Ex-ante funding and ex-post funding
questionBank.exp: Explicit DIS mandates range from narrow Pay-Box systems, through Pay-Box with extended mandate and Least Cost, up to broad Risk Minimizer mandates. The funding-type pairing is a plausible-sounding distractor because ex-ante/ex-post is also presented as a spectrum in the material, but it describes funding timing, not mandate scope. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurance scheme owned jointly by government and private-sector shareholders illustrates which type of ownership structure?
opts: Private ownership
Joint ownership
Public ownership
Mutual ownership
questionBank.exp: Joint ownership specifically describes a DIS held by both private and public sectors together, distinct from schemes owned purely by one side. Public ownership is the closest wrong answer since government involvement is present in both, but public ownership means government holds the scheme exclusively. See 'Ownership' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Under which type of deposit insurance membership rule can a licensed bank legally decline to join the scheme?
opts: Compulsory membership
Voluntary membership
Risk-based membership
Provisional membership
questionBank.exp: Voluntary membership allows banks to opt in or out, in contrast to compulsory membership where banks have no choice. Compulsory membership is the natural contrasting distractor and is in fact the approach NDIC itself uses, which makes this pairing useful for testing the distinction. See 'Membership' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer extends coverage to non-bank institutions that accept deposit-like products, alongside licensed banks. Which goal does this primarily serve?
opts: Reducing the total premium income the insurer collects
Avoiding competitive distortions between similar deposit-taking institutions
Limiting the insurer's on-site examination workload
Concentrating deposit insurance risk in fewer institutions
questionBank.exp: Including non-bank deposit-taking institutions avoids competitive distortions between institutions offering similar products, while also strengthening overall financial-system stability. Concentrating risk in fewer institutions is the opposite of what broader participation does, but it can sound plausible if a reader is thinking about risk pooling in the wrong direction. See 'Participating Institutions' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Why does a deposit insurer typically require foreign-owned banks operating in its country to participate in the domestic deposit insurance scheme?
opts: To exempt foreign banks from domestic prudential supervision
To place foreign banks on equal competitive footing
To restrict foreign banks from accepting local currency deposits
To transfer foreign banks' deposit risk to their home regulator
questionBank.exp: One of the stated reasons foreign banks participate is to minimize competitive issues by placing them on equal footing with domestic banks, alongside stabilizing the domestic financial system. Exempting them from supervision is the opposite of what participation entails, but it can seem plausible if 'foreign' is read as implying special treatment. See 'Foreign Banks' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurance rule specifies that only certain account types qualify for protection, while a separate rule caps the amount payable per depositor. Which two coverage dimensions does this represent, respectively?
opts: Limits and scope
Scope and limits
Membership and assessment
Eligibility and assessment
questionBank.exp: Scope refers to which types of deposits are covered, while limits refer to the amounts covered -- the stem describes exactly this pairing in that order. The reversed-order option is the classic 'sounds right but backwards' trap: scope governs deposit types, not amounts. See 'Coverage: Scope & Limits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor is told that 100% of their deposit is protected, but only for certain specified deposit types. Which level of coverage does this describe?
opts: Blanket coverage
Full deposit coverage
Limited deposit coverage
Pass-through coverage
questionBank.exp: Full deposit coverage protects 100% of the deposit amount but only for specified deposit types -- distinct from blanket coverage, which extends to all depositors and all creditors regardless of type. Blanket coverage is the natural distractor since both involve full/complete protection language, but blanket coverage is broader in whose claims it covers. See 'Coverage: Scope & Limits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor holds funds in a savings account and separately pledges a collateral deposit against a loan at the same bank. If that bank fails, which of these two balances is eligible for deposit insurance payout?
opts: The collateral deposit balance
The savings account balance
Both balances in full
Neither of the two balances
questionBank.exp: Savings accounts are insurable deposits, while a deposit held as collateral against the depositor's own loan is excluded, since it functions as a counterclaim rather than a true deposit balance. Claiming 'both balances' is attractive because it treats every bank balance as equally insurable, which is exactly the assumption the collateral exclusion rule exists to correct. See the coverage examples table and 'Insurable Deposits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer collects small annual premiums from member banks every year, then draws on a larger reserve only if an actual bank failure occurs. Which funding approach does this describe?
opts: Ex-ante funding
Hybrid funding
Ex-post funding
Risk-based funding
questionBank.exp: Hybrid funding combines small regular contributions collected before any failure with a larger draw when a failure event actually happens -- the FDIC is cited as an example of this approach. Ex-ante funding is the closest wrong answer since it also involves collecting funds before failure, but it does not include the ex-post large-amount component described in the stem. See 'Funding & Assessment' in the manual.

questionBank.q: When calculating how much premium a bank must pay, which two possible bases can a deposit insurer apply the assessment rate to?
opts: Total assets or total liabilities
Total deposits or insurable deposits
Capital reserves or loan portfolio
Net income or shareholder equity
questionBank.exp: The assessment base for calculating premiums can be either a bank's total deposits or just its insurable deposits, depending on the scheme's design. Total assets/liabilities is a plausible-sounding financial pairing, but the assessment base is specifically deposit-focused, not a broader balance-sheet measure. See 'Assessment Base' in the manual.

questionBank.q: One premium assessment approach charges every bank the same rate regardless of risk, while another varies the rate based on each bank's riskiness. Which two approaches does this describe, respectively?
opts: Differential Premium Assessment System and Flat Rate
Flat Rate and Differential Premium Assessment System
Ex-ante funding and Ex-post funding methods
Risk Minimizer and Pay-Box insurance mandates
questionBank.exp: Flat Rate charges one uniform rate to all institutions, while the Differential Premium Assessment System (DPAS) varies rates according to individual bank risk -- exactly the order the stem presents them in. The reversed-order option again functions as the 'right terms, wrong order' trap. See 'Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer applies a flat-rate premium of 0.5% to each bank's insurable deposits. If a bank holds ₦40 million in insurable deposits, what premium is that bank required to pay?
questionBank.exp: 0.5% of ₦40 million is ₦200,000 (40,000,000 x 0.005). The ₦400,000 option comes from mistakenly doubling the rate to 1%, a common calculation slip when converting a percentage. This mirrors the flat-rate approach where every bank pays the same percentage of its insurable deposits regardless of risk. See 'Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A well-managed, low-risk bank pays the same deposit insurance premium rate as a poorly-managed, high-risk bank under its insurer's assessment system. Which criticism of that system does this scenario illustrate?
opts: It increases the insurer's administrative complexity
It makes safer banks subsidize weaker ones
It requires more frequent bank examinations
It reduces the insurer's total premium income
questionBank.exp: Under a flat-rate system, riskier banks pay the same rate as safer ones, meaning well-managed banks effectively subsidize weaker ones -- one of the system's core disadvantages, alongside reduced incentive for sound risk management. Increased administrative complexity is actually a criticism of the alternative (DPAS), not flat rate, which makes it a tempting but reversed distractor. See 'Flat Rate' advantages/disadvantages table in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurance fund's investment policy prioritizes safety and liquidity above return, and treats shares as an unsuitable asset class. Which objective does this policy primarily protect?
opts: Its ability to maximize shareholder dividend payments
Its ability to provide liquidity for deposit insurance responsibilities
Its ability to compete with commercial bank investment returns
Its ability to expand into new asset management markets
questionBank.exp: The fund's investment policy exists to preserve capital and ensure liquidity so the insurer can meet its deposit-payout obligations, which is exactly why shares are considered unsafe for the fund despite potentially higher returns. Maximizing dividend payments is off-target since the fund is not structured to generate shareholder dividends at all. See 'Fund Investment Policy' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurance system pays claims only up to a fixed maximum per depositor rather than reimbursing every naira on deposit. Which core policy objective does this design choice reflect?
opts: Maximizing premium revenue collected from member banks
Protecting small depositors from losing their savings
Reducing the central bank's lender-of-last-resort exposure
Standardizing capital adequacy ratios across all banks
questionBank.exp: Because limited coverage typically leaves the great majority of ordinary savers fully protected, the policy is designed around safeguarding small depositors rather than every creditor. Reducing lender-of-last-resort exposure is a plausible-sounding link since both are safety-net tools, but coverage limits are not designed to manage central bank liquidity risk. See 'DIS: Policy Objectives' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which single outcome is the most important macro-level objective of a deposit insurance system?
opts: Maximum profitability for the deposit insurance fund
Financial system stability through public confidence
Reduction of statutory cash reserve requirements
Full nationalization of the domestic banking sector
questionBank.exp: The manual states explicitly that the most important macro-objective of a DIS is financial system stability, achieved mainly by enhancing public confidence. Reducing cash reserve requirements is a real regulatory tool, but it belongs to monetary policy, not the stated purpose of deposit insurance. See 'DIS: Policy Objectives' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a specific reason why deposit insurance exists?
opts: To increase banks' minimum capital requirements
To minimize the adverse impact of bank failure
To transfer bank supervision to the finance ministry
To reduce the number of licensed banks nationwide
questionBank.exp: Minimizing the adverse impact of bank failure is one of four reasons for deposit insurance given in the manual, alongside completing the safety net and formalizing the shift from implicit to explicit protection. Reducing the number of licensed banks is a plausible-sounding regulatory goal, but it is not among the stated reasons for deposit insurance itself. See 'Reasons for Deposit Insurance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Deposit insurance itself is which type of element within the broader financial safety net?
opts: A replacement for the financial safety net
A component of the financial safety net
An alternative to prudential supervision
A substitute for central bank lending
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance is explicitly framed as one component of the financial safety net, working alongside regulation/supervision and lender-of-last-resort facilities, not replacing them. Calling it a substitute for central bank lending is tempting because both cushion against failure, but the manual is clear that DI complements rather than replaces the other pillars. See 'Reasons for Deposit Insurance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer begins extending insurance coverage to mobile phone airtime balances held with licensed institutions, in addition to traditional bank deposits. What is this action an example of?
opts: Imposing a systemic blanket guarantee
Expanding coverage beyond traditional deposit products
Adopting a differential premium assessment system
Converting to an implicit deposit insurance scheme
questionBank.exp: Expanding insurance beyond traditional bank deposit products to items such as mobile phone airtime is explicitly listed as a way DIS maintains and reinforces public confidence. A blanket guarantee is a tempting distractor because it is also a confidence-building tool, but it means extending protection to all depositors and creditors during a crisis, not adding new product types to coverage. See 'Enhancing Public Confidence' in the manual.

questionBank.q: How does educating depositors about their deposit insurance rights strengthen the broader banking system?
opts: Educated depositors qualify for higher coverage limits
Informed depositors can impose additional market discipline on banks
Financial literacy reduces a bank's statutory premium rate
Informed depositors are exempted from deposit insurance fees
questionBank.exp: Financially literate depositors who know their rights can scrutinize bank conduct and practices, adding a layer of market discipline beyond formal supervision. Reduced premium rates is an appealing but incorrect link, since depositor education does not factor into how a bank's premium is calculated. See 'Enhancing Public Confidence' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer signals it will pursue legal action against bank directors found responsible for improper conduct that contributed to a failure. Which broader goal does this support?
opts: Increasing the deposit insurance fund's investment returns
Mitigating moral hazard through accountability
Simplifying the premium assessment formula
Reducing the insurer's on-site examination frequency
questionBank.exp: A demonstrated willingness to take legal action against directors for improper acts is listed as one specific design feature that mitigates moral hazard, alongside limits on coverage and sound risk management. Reducing examination frequency runs in the opposite direction of accountability-focused deterrence, making it an attractive but wrong pairing. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Alongside a sound legal regime, which of the following is also listed as a condition necessary for deposit insurance to operate effectively?
opts: Universal blanket coverage for all depositors
Sound accounting and financial reporting regimes
A single state-owned deposit insurer
Unlimited central bank recapitalization
questionBank.exp: Sound accounting and financial reporting regimes are listed alongside a sound legal regime, strong prudential regulation and supervision, and comprehensive bank disclosure as the four conditions for effective deposit insurance. Universal blanket coverage sounds protective, but permanent blanket coverage is explicitly discouraged as best practice, not treated as a precondition for effectiveness. See 'Conditions for Effective DI' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a genuine merit of an implicit, discretionary deposit insurance approach compared to an explicit one?
opts: Faster response to crises due to pre-approved budgets
Flexibility in setting the scope of protection
Lower moral hazard than a typical explicit scheme
Reduced need for premium collection from healthy banks
questionBank.exp: Implicit DIS's genuine, stated merit is the flexibility it gives authorities to set the level, scope, and extent of protection at their discretion. 'Faster response due to pre-approved budgets' is actually a reversal of a real shortcoming -- implicit schemes are criticized for slow responses precisely because of budgetary debate, not pre-approval. See 'Merits & Shortcomings of Implicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Approximately how many countries' deposit insurance systems rely on explicit, limited coverage?
questionBank.exp: The manual states that most countries rely on explicit, limited deposit insurance -- 108 systems worldwide. The other numbers are real figures from elsewhere in the material (52 banks under Holding Actions, 24 banks taken over 1991-1996, 49 total failed banks) that are easy to confuse if the numbers are not anchored to their specific context. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor holds a joint savings account and separately holds units in a mutual fund at the same institution. Under standard deposit insurance coverage rules, which of these two holdings is insurable?
opts: The mutual fund units
The joint savings account
Both holdings in full
Neither holding qualifies for coverage
questionBank.exp: Joint and savings accounts are insurable deposits, while mutual fund investments are explicitly excluded from deposit insurance coverage since they are investment products, not deposits. Claiming both holdings are covered is the natural over-inclusive trap the coverage-examples table is designed to correct. See the coverage examples table in the manual.

questionBank.q: Under which funding arrangement does a deposit insurer collect no funds from member banks until after a specific bank has already failed?
opts: Ex-ante funding
Ex-post funding
Hybrid funding
Differential premium funding
questionBank.exp: Ex-post funding collects contributions from surviving banks only after a failure has occurred, in contrast to ex-ante funding, which builds a fund in advance through regular premiums. Hybrid funding is a tempting middle-ground distractor, but it still involves some small annual collection before any failure, unlike pure ex-post funding. See 'Types of Funding' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What two factors primarily determine the assessment rate a deposit insurer applies to calculate premiums?
opts: The bank's total assets and its number of branches
The scheme's age and the fund's obligation level
The country's inflation rate and exchange rate
The bank's credit rating and shareholder structure
questionBank.exp: The assessment rate depends on the age of the deposit insurance system and the status of the deposit insurance fund relative to its level of obligation -- younger or more exposed funds typically need higher rates. A bank's credit rating sounds relevant to risk pricing, but the manual ties the rate to the fund's own maturity and exposure, not to individual bank credit ratings. See 'Assessment Rate' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a genuine advantage of the Differential Premium Assessment System over a flat-rate system?
opts: It requires less detailed information from banks
It encourages banks to adopt sound risk management practices
It is simpler to implement initially than a flat rate
It removes the need to classify banks by risk
questionBank.exp: Because DPAS ties premiums to individual bank risk, it creates a direct financial incentive for banks to manage risk soundly -- this is one of its stated advantages, along with fairness and reduced moral hazard. Claiming it is simpler to implement is a direct reversal of a real listed disadvantage: DPAS is explicitly described as difficult to implement initially and information-intensive. See 'Differential Premium Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer using a risk-based premium system finds that classifying banks into consistent risk clusters is genuinely difficult and information-intensive to sustain. Which documented drawback of that system does this reflect?
opts: The tendency to subsidize weaker banks with safer banks' premiums
The complexity of classifying banks into risk clusters
The lack of incentive for banks to manage risk soundly
The protection it gives risky banks from public identification
questionBank.exp: The manual lists the complexity of classifying banks into risk clusters as one of DPAS's specific disadvantages, alongside its heavy information requirements. Subsidizing weaker banks, lack of risk-management incentive, and shielding risky banks from identification are all real criticisms -- but they describe the flat-rate system, not DPAS, making this a reversed-attribution trap. See 'Differential Premium Assessment Approach' and 'Flat Rate' tables in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurance scheme is owned and funded entirely by private-sector financial institutions, with no government shareholding. Which ownership structure does this describe?
opts: Public ownership
Private ownership
Joint ownership
Mutual ownership
questionBank.exp: Private ownership describes a scheme purely owned by the private sector, distinct from public ownership (government-only) or joint ownership (both sectors together). 'Mutual ownership' is a plausible-sounding but unlisted category, easily confused with the genuine three-way classification the manual actually gives. See 'Ownership' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer requires a licensed microfinance bank to meet the same prudential regulatory standards as a commercial bank because both accept deposits from the public. Which rationale for broad institutional participation does this reflect?
opts: Reducing the microfinance bank's premium obligations
Applying consistent prudential rules across similar institutions
Exempting the microfinance bank from deposit insurance membership
Transferring supervisory authority to the commercial bank
questionBank.exp: One stated reason for including non-bank deposit-taking institutions is the desire to apply prudential regulatory and supervisory rules consistently to all institutions accepting deposits, alongside avoiding competitive distortion and strengthening stability. Exempting the microfinance bank is the opposite of what consistent-rules participation achieves, but it can sound plausible if 'different institution type' is read as implying special treatment. See 'Participating Institutions' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer includes foreign-owned banks as members partly to broaden the pool of institutions paying into the fund. Which rationale for foreign bank participation does this reflect?
opts: Restricting foreign banks' access to domestic currency markets
Encouraging diversification that comes from a wider membership base
Reducing the total number of licensed institutions
Consolidating foreign banks under a single regulator
questionBank.exp: Wider membership from foreign banks expands and diversifies the insurer's funding base, one of five stated reasons for including them alongside stability and competitive-footing arguments. Reducing the number of licensed institutions runs opposite to the diversification goal, but it can seem plausible if 'inclusion' is mistakenly read as a consolidation measure. See 'Foreign Banks' in the manual.

questionBank.q: During a systemic banking crisis, a country's authorities temporarily extend a blanket guarantee to all depositors and creditors, beyond the normal insured limit. Which purpose does this action mainly serve?
opts: Replacing deposit insurance permanently
Stabilizing the financial system during a crisis
Standardizing the premium assessment formula
Reducing the insurer's need for a legal mandate
questionBank.exp: Blanket guarantees are listed as a systemic stabilization measure used to reinforce confidence during periods of severe crisis -- a temporary, extraordinary tool, not a permanent replacement for ordinary deposit insurance. Framing it as replacing deposit insurance permanently is the natural but incorrect over-extension of what is actually a time-limited emergency measure. See 'Enhancing Public Confidence' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which description best matches the definition of a 'bank run'?
opts: A scheduled bulk transfer of deposits between two merging banks
A large-scale withdrawal of deposits driven by fear that a bank may fail
A routine audit of a bank's deposit records by examiners
A gradual decline in a bank's deposit base over several years
questionBank.exp: A bank run is specifically a large-scale, fear-driven withdrawal of deposits, precipitated by concern that a bank may fail and depositors may suffer losses -- distinct from routine or gradual deposit movements. A gradual multi-year decline sounds similar because it also involves falling deposits, but it lacks the panic-driven, large-scale character that defines a run. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which term refers to the risk that the failure of one financial institution could cascade into the collapse of the entire financial system?
opts: Moral hazard
Systemic risk
Adverse selection
Depositor preference
questionBank.exp: Systemic risk specifically concerns collapse of an entire system or market through cascading failures, distinguishing it from moral hazard (excessive risk-taking) and adverse selection (self-selection into coverage). Depositor preference is an unrelated liquidation-priority concept, included here as a plausible-sounding but mismatched term. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A bank's total deposits are ₦900 million, of which ₦150 million are staff and director deposits excluded from coverage. If the insurer uses the insurable-deposits assessment base, what figure does it apply the premium rate to?
opts: ₦900 million
₦750 million
₦150 million
₦1,050 million
questionBank.exp: Using the insurable-deposits base means the premium rate applies only to deposits eligible for coverage -- total deposits minus excluded categories such as insider deposits, which is 900 million minus 150 million, or 750 million naira. Applying the rate to the full 900 million is the natural mistake of using the total-deposits base instead of the insurable-deposits base the question specifies. See 'Assessment Base' and 'Insurable Deposits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: An insurer protects 100% of deposits for all account types held by every depositor and creditor of a failed bank, without exception. Which level of coverage does this represent?
opts: Full deposit coverage
Blanket coverage
Limited deposit coverage
Pass-through coverage
questionBank.exp: Blanket coverage is the broadest level, extending full protection to all depositors and all creditors without exception -- distinct from full deposit coverage, which protects 100% of deposits but only for specified deposit types, not all creditors. Full deposit coverage is the closest wrong answer since both involve 100% protection, but it does not extend to all creditors the way blanket coverage does. See 'Coverage: Scope & Limits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Beyond the maximum insured amount, what other two elements does an explicit deposit insurance scheme typically specify in law or contract?
opts: The bank's dividend policy and executive compensation
The funding arrangement and scheme administration
The central bank's interest rate corridor
The national budget allocation for infrastructure
questionBank.exp: An explicit scheme specifies the maximum insured amount, the funding arrangement, and how the scheme is administered -- giving depositors certainty and clear standards. Dividend policy and executive compensation are real corporate-governance topics, but they are not among the elements a deposit insurance scheme itself specifies. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A country's banking sector is stable, and regulators value the ability to respond to problem banks with maximum discretion rather than pre-committed rules. Which type of deposit insurance approach best fits this stated preference, even though it carries recognized shortcomings?
opts: Explicit deposit insurance
Implicit deposit insurance
A risk minimizer mandate
A differential premium assessment system
questionBank.exp: Implicit deposit insurance's core, stated merit is exactly this: flexibility to set the level, scope, and extent of protection at the authorities' discretion, which suits a preference for case-by-case judgment over fixed rules. Explicit deposit insurance is the natural contrasting choice, but it operates through codified, pre-committed rules rather than the maximum discretion this scenario describes. See 'Merits & Shortcomings of Implicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: 'Deposit' and 'eligible deposits' are related but distinct terms. What does the narrower term, eligible deposits, specifically refer to?
opts: Any credit balance resulting from funds left in an account
Deposits meeting the requirements for insurance coverage
Deposits held as collateral for a loan at the same institution
Deposits that exceed the maximum insured coverage limit
questionBank.exp: Eligible deposits are specifically those that fall within the scope of coverage -- meeting the type-of-depositor and type-of-deposit requirements -- narrower than the general definition of 'deposit' itself, which covers any credit balance a financial institution must repay. Option A is actually the glossary's definition of the broader term 'deposit,' not the narrower 'eligible deposits,' making it an attractive but mismatched answer. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A newly-established deposit insurer cites 'promoting competition amongst banks by guaranteeing all depositors regardless of institution' as one of its founding goals. This goal is classified as which type of statement?
opts: A condition for effective deposit insurance
A deposit insurance policy objective
A moral hazard mitigation measure
A failure resolution principle
questionBank.exp: Promoting competition among banks by guaranteeing all depositors regardless of institution is listed specifically among the DIS Policy Objectives, alongside protecting small depositors and contributing to financial stability. Calling it a moral hazard mitigation measure is tempting since both concern how coverage rules shape bank behavior, but moral hazard mitigation is about limiting risk-taking incentives, not equalizing competitive conditions. See 'DIS: Policy Objectives' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A bank strengthens its own board oversight and internal risk controls partly because deposit insurance has reduced depositors' incentive to monitor the bank themselves. Which moral hazard mitigation measure does this illustrate?
opts: A differential premium assessment system
Good corporate governance and sound risk management
A statutory cap on the deposit insurance fund's size
A mandatory blanket guarantee for all depositors
questionBank.exp: Good corporate governance and sound risk management by individual banks is explicitly listed as the first measure for mitigating moral hazard, working alongside market discipline and regulatory frameworks. A blanket guarantee is the opposite of a mitigation measure here, since it is a systemic tool that can itself increase risky behavior if used too broadly. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Large uninsured creditors and shareholders actively monitor a bank's risk-taking because they stand to lose money if it fails. Which moral hazard mitigation channel does this represent?
opts: A formal risk minimizer supervisory mandate structure
Market discipline from shareholders and larger creditors
A pass-through insurance arrangement for pooled accounts
An ex-post premium collection system for insurers
questionBank.exp: Market discipline exercised by shareholders and larger creditors, who have strong incentives to monitor a bank's risk-taking, is explicitly listed as a moral hazard mitigation channel alongside governance and regulation. A pass-through arrangement is a real DI concept but concerns extending coverage through pooled accounts, not monitoring incentives. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a mitigation channel for moral hazard, alongside good corporate governance and market discipline?
opts: Unlimited coverage for all classes of depositors
Effective frameworks for strong prudential regulation and supervision
Voluntary membership for all licensed banks
A single flat premium rate for every institution
questionBank.exp: Strong prudential regulation and supervision frameworks are listed as a core moral hazard mitigation channel, complementing governance and market discipline. Unlimited coverage is the opposite of a mitigation measure, since broader, uncapped protection typically increases moral hazard rather than reducing it. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A regulator intervenes to close a struggling bank while it still has some remaining asset value, rather than allowing it to continue operating until it is fully insolvent. Which moral hazard mitigation goal does this early action serve?
opts: Maximizing the failing bank's remaining shareholder dividends
Minimizing loss through early closure of troubled banks
Extending the bank's deposit insurance coverage limit
Postponing the troubled bank's premium assessment date
questionBank.exp: Minimizing the risk of loss through early closure of a troubled bank is explicitly listed as a moral hazard mitigation design feature, since delaying intervention lets losses and risky behavior compound. Extending coverage limits runs in the opposite direction of loss-minimization, but it can sound protective if 'reducing risk to depositors' is confused with 'reducing risk to the fund.' See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A country already has strong bank supervision and a central bank lender-of-last-resort facility, but adds deposit insurance to complete its protective framework. Which stated reason for deposit insurance does this reflect?
opts: Formalizing the transition from implicit to explicit protection
Ensuring the completeness of the financial safety-net arrangement
Minimizing the adverse impact of bank failure
Promoting competition among licensed banks
questionBank.exp: Ensuring the completeness of the financial safety-net arrangement is one of the four stated reasons for deposit insurance -- it is the piece that rounds out supervision and lender-of-last-resort support into a full safety net. The other reasons listed are real but describe different situations: formalizing a transition applies when replacing implicit protection, not adding a missing third pillar. See 'Reasons for Deposit Insurance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Beyond protecting depositors, which broader set of outcomes does deposit insurance promote for the wider economy?
opts: Lower interest rates and reduced government borrowing
Confidence, good savings habits, and economic growth
Higher stock market valuations and export growth
Reduced income inequality and lower unemployment
questionBank.exp: The manual states that deposit insurance promotes confidence, good savings habits, and economic growth as part of the financial safety net's broader function. Lower interest rates and reduced government borrowing sound like plausible macroeconomic benefits, but they are not among the outcomes the manual attributes to deposit insurance. See 'Financial Safety Net' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor in a country with an explicit, codified deposit insurance scheme knows in advance exactly how much of their balance is protected and how claims will be handled. Which benefit of explicit DIS does this illustrate?
opts: It shifts capital reserve duties to the central bank
It provides depositors with certainty about their protection
It transfers all bank supervision duties to the deposit insurer
It removes the bank's requirement to pay deposit insurance premiums
questionBank.exp: Explicit deposit insurance provides depositors with certainty about their protection precisely because the rules, limits, and procedures are codified in advance, unlike the ambiguity of implicit protection. Transferring all supervision duties to the insurer is a plausible-sounding overreach, but explicit DIS coexists with, rather than replaces, separate prudential supervision arrangements. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What is a 'blanket guarantee'?
opts: A statutory cap on the deposit insurance fund's total size
A declaration extending protection beyond normal limited coverage
A contractual agreement between two merging banks
A routine periodic review of a bank's asset quality
questionBank.exp: The glossary defines a blanket guarantee as a declaration by authorities that, beyond normal limited-coverage deposit insurance, certain deposits and possibly other financial instruments will be protected -- a temporary, extraordinary measure. A contractual merger agreement is unrelated to guarantee declarations, though the word 'agreement' can create false association. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: Prudential regulation and supervision, resolution mechanisms including lender-of-last-resort support, and deposit insurance are combined under which single umbrella term?
opts: Systemic stabilization framework
The financial safety-net
Deposit insurance system
Bank supervisory regime
questionBank.exp: The financial safety-net is the combined function of prudential regulation and supervision, resolution mechanisms (including lender-of-last-resort support), and deposit insurance working together to create an orderly financial system. 'Systemic stabilization framework' sounds like a plausible synonym, but it is not the term the glossary actually assigns to this combination. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer decides that premiums will be calculated as a percentage of each bank's total deposits rather than a fixed fee per branch. What is the technical term for the deposit figure the rate is multiplied against?
opts: Assessment rate
Assessment base
Premium ceiling
Capital adequacy ratio
questionBank.exp: The assessment base is the specific value -- total deposits or insurable deposits -- to which the deposit insurer applies its assessment rate to calculate the premium owed. 'Assessment rate' is a closely related but distinct term: it is the percentage applied to the base, not the base itself. See the Glossary of Terms and 'Assessment Base' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which term describes a premium assessment approach that links each bank's premium to its individual risk profile or other specific criteria?
opts: Flat rate system
Differential premium system
Ex-ante funding system
Pass-through insurance system
questionBank.exp: A differential premium system, also called a risk-based premium system, links premiums directly to each bank's individual risk profile or other defined criteria, in contrast to a flat rate that ignores risk entirely. 'Ex-ante funding' is a plausible-sounding pairing since both concern how premiums are structured, but ex-ante describes funding timing, not risk-based pricing. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer notices that the healthiest, best-capitalized banks in its country consistently choose not to join its voluntary scheme, while weaker banks eagerly sign up. What is this phenomenon called?
opts: Moral hazard
Selection bias
Depositor preference
Systemic stabilization
questionBank.exp: The glossary term for this exact pattern -- higher-risk institutions opting in while lower-risk ones opt out under a voluntary scheme -- is selection bias, also referred to as adverse selection. Moral hazard is the closely related but distinct sibling concept: it concerns risk-taking behavior after coverage exists, not which institutions choose to join. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: In deposit insurance terminology, what is the 'premium'?
opts: The maximum amount a depositor can claim after a bank failure
What a member bank pays for coverage in a period
The interest rate a central bank charges for emergency lending
The percentage of a bank's assets held in liquid reserves
questionBank.exp: The premium is the amount a member institution pays for deposit insurance over a given period, such as a year -- the funding mechanism that supports the deposit insurance fund. The maximum claim amount is a different concept entirely (the insured limit), which makes it a tempting mix-up since both are monetary figures tied to deposit insurance. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer applies a base differential premium rate of 0.7% to a bank's deposits, then adds a 0.2 percentage point risk surcharge for a bank with a high proportion of bad loans. If that bank holds ₦600 million in assessable deposits, what total premium rate is applied to it?
questionBank.exp: Adding the 0.2 percentage point risk surcharge to the 0.7% base rate gives a total differential premium rate of 0.9% for this higher-risk bank -- exactly how the Differential Premium Assessment System raises rates for riskier institutions above the base premium rate. Selecting 0.7% would mean ignoring the risk add-on entirely, defeating the purpose of a differential system. See 'Assessment Approach' and the flat-versus-differential worked example in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor holds a current account and separately holds units in a mutual fund investment, both at the same bank. If the bank fails, which of these two holdings is eligible for deposit insurance payout?
opts: The mutual fund units
The current account
Both holdings in full
Neither holding qualifies for coverage
questionBank.exp: Current accounts are explicitly listed as an insurable deposit type, while mutual fund investments are excluded from deposit insurance coverage since they are investment products rather than deposits. Claiming both holdings are covered repeats the natural over-inclusive assumption the coverage-examples table is designed to correct. See the coverage examples table in the manual.

questionBank.q: If tasked with designing a new deposit insurance scheme from scratch, which set of elements would a design-features framework direct you to decide first?
opts: Interest rates, exchange rates, and inflation targets
Ownership, membership, participating institutions, coverage, and funding
Bank branch locations and staffing levels
Shareholder dividend policy and executive pay
questionBank.exp: The manual's 'Design Features of Deposit Insurance Scheme' section frames the key design decisions around ownership, membership, participating institutions, coverage, and funding -- the core structural choices that shape how a scheme operates. Interest rates and inflation targets are macroeconomic policy levers, not part of the DIS design-features framework itself. See 'Design Features of Deposit Insurance Scheme' in the manual.

questionBank.q: When a bank fails under an explicit deposit insurance system, the insurer can draw on a pre-established fund rather than negotiating emergency financing after the fact. Which stated benefit of explicit DIS does this represent?
opts: An unlimited legal mandate over monetary policy
Ready access to funds when a bank fails
A permanent exemption from failure resolution procedures
A fixed schedule of bank merger approvals
questionBank.exp: Explicit deposit insurance provides ready access to funds when a bank fails, since the insurer draws on a pre-established fund rather than arranging emergency financing after the fact -- one of its stated advantages over implicit protection. An unlimited monetary policy mandate is an unrelated overreach, though 'unlimited' can sound like a natural extension of 'ready access to funds.' See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which safety-net function provides temporary emergency liquidity support specifically to solvent depository institutions, rather than compensating depositors directly?
opts: Deposit insurance protection
The lender-of-last-resort facility
Prudential regulation and supervision
Bank liquidation proceedings
questionBank.exp: The lender-of-last-resort facility, typically provided by the central bank, gives temporary emergency liquidity specifically to solvent institutions facing short-term funding pressure, distinct from deposit insurance, which compensates depositors after a failure. Prudential supervision is a plausible-sounding distractor since it is also a safety-net pillar, but it concerns ongoing oversight, not emergency liquidity provision. See 'Financial Safety Net' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Regulators in Country A pass a law specifying a fixed insured limit, a dedicated fund, and clear payout procedures before any bank fails. Regulators in Country B instead decide case-by-case, after a bank gets into trouble, how much support to provide. Which pairing correctly matches each country to its deposit protection type?
opts: A is implicit; B is explicit
A is explicit; B is implicit
Both countries use blanket coverage
Both countries use pass-through insurance
questionBank.exp: Country A's advance legal specification of limits, funding, and procedures is the hallmark of explicit deposit insurance, while Country B's case-by-case, after-the-fact decision-making is exactly how implicit deposit insurance is described. The reversed pairing is the natural 'right concepts, wrong assignment' trap this kind of matching question is designed to catch. See 'Implicit DIS' and 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Two banks each hold ₦1 billion in assessable deposits. Bank X pays a flat rate of 0.5%. Bank Y pays a differential rate of 0.9% because of its higher risk profile. How much more does Bank Y pay in premium than Bank X?
questionBank.exp: Bank X pays 0.5% of 1 billion naira, or 5,000,000; Bank Y pays 0.9%, or 9,000,000 -- a difference of 4,000,000 naira. Choosing 9,000,000 mistakes Bank Y's full premium for the difference between the two banks' premiums. This illustrates exactly why the Differential Premium Assessment System raises costs for riskier banks relative to a flat-rate baseline. See 'Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A fundamentally solvent bank faces a short-term cash crunch due to a temporary funding mismatch, not because it is failing. Which safety-net function is designed to address exactly this situation?
opts: Deposit insurance payout
Lender-of-last-resort support
Bank liquidation
Purchase and assumption
questionBank.exp: Lender-of-last-resort support exists specifically to provide temporary liquidity to solvent institutions facing short-term funding pressure, which is precisely this scenario -- not a failure requiring deposit insurance or liquidation. Deposit insurance payout is the natural but incorrect reach, since it only activates once a bank has actually failed, not for a temporary liquidity mismatch in an otherwise sound bank. See 'Financial Safety Net' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A voluntary deposit insurance scheme attracts mostly high-risk banks, and those banks then take on even more risk once covered. Which two distinct problems are occurring together in this scenario?
opts: Systemic risk and depositor preference
Adverse selection and moral hazard
Blanket coverage and pass-through insurance
Ex-ante funding and ex-post funding
questionBank.exp: This scenario combines both classic DI design risks: adverse selection explains why high-risk banks disproportionately join a voluntary scheme, and moral hazard explains why those same banks then take on more risk once covered. Systemic risk and depositor preference are real terms but describe different phenomena entirely -- systemic contagion and liquidation-claim priority, not selection or risk-taking incentives. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' and 'DIS & Adverse Selection' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor's only account is a savings account with a balance of ₦300,000 at a bank whose insured limit is ₦500,000 per depositor. If that bank fails, how much of the depositor's balance is protected by deposit insurance?
opts: ₦500,000, the full insured limit regardless of balance
The full ₦300,000, since it's within the limit
₦200,000, the difference between the balance and the limit
Nothing, since savings accounts require a separate application for coverage
questionBank.exp: Because the account type (savings) is within scope and the balance of 300,000 naira falls below the 500,000 naira insured limit, the full balance is protected -- deposit insurance pays the lesser of the actual balance or the insured limit, not a fixed amount regardless of balance. Claiming automatic payment of the full insured limit is the natural but incorrect assumption that coverage always pays the maximum rather than the actual balance held. See 'Coverage - Claim' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer's board is entirely appointed by the finance ministry, and its capital comes solely from state funds. Which ownership structure does this describe?
opts: Private ownership
Public ownership
Joint ownership
Mutual ownership
questionBank.exp: Public ownership means government holds the deposit insurance scheme exclusively -- reflected here by a state-appointed board and state-only capital. Joint ownership is the natural contrasting distractor because government is involved in both, but joint ownership requires private-sector participation as well, which is absent from this scenario. See 'Ownership' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A regulator worries that under a voluntary deposit insurance scheme, only the riskiest banks will choose to join, undermining the fund's stability. Which membership rule would most directly address this specific concern?
opts: A higher insured coverage limit for all banks
Compulsory membership for all licensed banks
A blanket guarantee during a systemic crisis
A reduced flat-rate premium for new entrants
questionBank.exp: Making membership compulsory directly removes the ability of low-risk banks to opt out, which is exactly the adverse selection problem a voluntary scheme creates -- this is why compulsory membership is generally treated as best practice. A higher coverage limit does not address who joins the scheme at all, and can actually worsen moral hazard rather than solve the selection problem described. See 'Membership' and 'DIS & Adverse Selection' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A banking sector is expanding rapidly, and regulators are concerned that new entrants may take on excessive risk while relying on the safety net for protection. Which single design choice would most directly target this specific risk?
opts: Extending blanket coverage to all new entrant banks
A differential premium system tied to bank risk
Lowering the minimum capital requirement for new banks
Simplifying the licensing process for new entrant banks
questionBank.exp: A differential premium system directly ties the cost of coverage to each bank's actual risk profile, giving newer, potentially riskier entrants a direct financial incentive to manage risk soundly -- squarely targeting the moral hazard concern described. Extending blanket coverage would move in the opposite direction, increasing rather than reducing the incentive for excessive risk-taking. See 'DIS & Moral Hazard' and 'Differential Premium Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A financial safety net succeeds when depositors stop distinguishing between money held in a bank and money held as physical cash. Which single word names this end state?
opts: Liquidity
Confidence
Solvency
Stability
questionBank.exp: The manual defines confidence as being achieved precisely when a depositor believes that money in the bank is as good as money in their pocket -- the specific end state deposit insurance and the wider safety net are designed to produce. 'Stability' is a closely related but broader systemic outcome, whereas confidence specifically describes the individual depositor's psychological state. See 'Enhancing Public Confidence' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which statement reflects best practice regarding blanket and full deposit coverage?
opts: Every deposit insurance system eventually adopts blanket coverage
No deposit insurance system permanently adopts blanket or full coverage
Blanket coverage is required during a bank's first year of operation
Full deposit coverage is mandatory for all non-bank institutions
questionBank.exp: The manual states plainly that limited deposit coverage is best practice and that, in reality, no deposit insurance system adopts blanket or full coverage permanently -- those levels are used only temporarily, such as during a systemic crisis. Claiming every system eventually adopts blanket coverage reverses this stated principle entirely. See 'Coverage: Scope & Limits' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A foreign-owned bank operating domestically is required to join the local deposit insurance scheme partly because its failure could disrupt the host country's own financial system. Which rationale for foreign bank inclusion does this reflect?
opts: Reducing the foreign bank's home-country tax obligations
Ensuring the stability of the domestic financial system
Simplifying the foreign bank's cross-border reporting
Standardizing the foreign bank's executive compensation
questionBank.exp: Ensuring the stability of the domestic financial system is explicitly listed as one reason foreign banks participate, since a foreign bank's failure can threaten the host country regardless of where its parent is based. Reducing home-country tax obligations is unrelated to deposit insurance membership, though it may sound plausible as a general benefit of cross-border banking. See 'Foreign Banks' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer extends membership to any institution accepting deposit-like products, not just traditional banks, in order to strengthen overall system stability. Which rationale for participating institutions does this reflect?
opts: Reducing the total premium collected across the sector
Enhancing system stability by including all deposit-like providers
Restricting deposit insurance to the five largest banks
Exempting smaller institutions from prudential rules
questionBank.exp: Including all institutions that accept deposits or deposit-like products is explicitly listed as a way to enhance the stability of the financial system, alongside avoiding competitive distortion. Restricting coverage to only the largest banks runs directly opposite to this stability rationale, which depends on broad, consistent participation. See 'Participating Institutions' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Real-world Differential Premium Assessment System models typically combine measurable financial data with judgment-based factors like management quality. Which type of factor do these models generally weight more heavily?
opts: Qualitative factors
Quantitative factors
Historical factors
Reputational factors
questionBank.exp: DPAS models in practice show a preference for combining both quantitative and qualitative factors, but they generally give greater weight to quantitative measures such as capital ratios and asset quality. Qualitative factors like management quality are still used, but as a secondary weighting rather than the dominant one. See 'Premium: Types of Premium Assessment' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which benefit of explicit deposit insurance specifically concerns how much financial exposure the government itself retains when a bank fails?
opts: It transfers all bank ownership to the government
It limits the government's liabilities in handling bank failure
It removes the government's role in bank licensing
It increases the government's annual budget deficit
questionBank.exp: One of explicit DIS's stated benefits is that it limits the government's liabilities in handling bank failure, since the pre-funded scheme -- not the general treasury -- bears the cost. Transferring bank ownership to the government is an unrelated overreach, though 'government involvement' can create a loose association with this benefit. See 'Explicit DIS' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which term refers to measures such as blanket guarantees that are designed to prevent the collapse of an entire financial system?
opts: Systemic risk
Systemic stabilization
Financial inclusion
Depositor preference
questionBank.exp: Systemic stabilization refers to measures, such as blanket guarantees, designed specifically to prevent financial system collapse, distinguishing it from systemic risk, which describes the danger itself rather than the response to it. Financial inclusion is a real glossary term but concerns access to and use of formal financial services, an unrelated concept. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A supervisor requires a weakening bank to raise private capital and divest certain assets before its condition deteriorates further, aiming to help it return to normal business without needing formal resolution. What is this category of action called?
opts: Bank liquidation
Early intervention
Purchase and assumption
Systemic stabilization
questionBank.exp: Early intervention refers to remedial actions taken by supervisors or resolution authorities to correct irregularities early enough to help a bank return to normal business and avoid entering a resolution stage -- exactly the raising-capital, divesting-assets scenario described. Liquidation and purchase and assumption are both resolution-stage actions that occur after a bank has already failed, not preventive measures taken beforehand. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A regulator imposes a set of restrictions on a distressed bank -- barring new loans and requiring debt recovery efforts -- specifically to stop or reverse its decline. What is this category of measure called?
opts: Open bank assistance
Holding actions
Failure resolution
Depositor reimbursement
questionBank.exp: Holding actions are a series of measures imposed on distressed banks -- such as barring new loans and pursuing debt recovery -- specifically to stop or reverse a decline in their condition. Open bank assistance is a closely related but distinct concept: it involves broader therapies like financial support and management changes to help a failing bank continue as a going concern, not just restrictive measures. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A regulator assesses whether a proposed bank director has the competence, integrity, and track record needed for the role before approving the appointment. What is this assessment process called?
opts: A formal capital adequacy assessment process
A fit and proper test
A routine prudential examination process
A standard risk minimizer review process
questionBank.exp: Fit and proper tests specifically assess a manager or director's competence to fulfill their responsibilities (fitness) and their integrity and suitability (propriety), often based on qualifications, experience, and track record. A prudential examination is a plausible-sounding distractor since both involve regulatory scrutiny, but examinations assess a bank's overall financial condition, not an individual's suitability for a role. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor's ₦2 million balance in an insurable account exceeds the ₦500,000 insured limit at their failed bank. After the insurer pays the ₦500,000 insured sum, what additional recovery mechanism might return some or all of the remaining ₦1.5 million to the depositor?
opts: A second, higher deposit insurance payout from the same insurer
Liquidation dividends from the failed bank's asset sales
A mandatory blanket guarantee for this specific bank
A refund of the depositor's premium contributions
questionBank.exp: Beyond the insured sum, uninsured depositors can recover additional amounts through liquidation dividends -- payments made from the proceeds of selling the failed bank's assets and recovering its debts. Suggesting a second, higher insurance payout misunderstands how coverage works: the insured limit is a hard cap on the insurance payout itself, with any further recovery coming from asset realization, not additional insurance funds. See 'DI Coverage - Liquidation Dividends' in the manual.

questionBank.q: 'A sound and effective legal regime' and 'strong prudential regulation and supervision' are both examples of which category of statement?
opts: Reasons why deposit insurance is established
Conditions for effective deposit insurance
Design features determining coverage limits
Types of premium assessment approaches
questionBank.exp: A sound legal regime and strong prudential regulation and supervision are both listed among the four conditions the manual identifies as necessary for deposit insurance to function effectively, distinct from the separate list of reasons deposit insurance is established in the first place. Confusing 'conditions for effectiveness' with 'reasons for existence' is an easy mix-up since both lists describe foundational aspects of DIS. See 'Conditions for Effective DI' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following topics belongs to institution-specific detail about Nigeria's deposit insurer rather than the general theory of deposit insurance covered so far?
opts: The general distinction between implicit and explicit deposit insurance
NDIC's ownership split between the CBN and MOFI
The general concept of moral hazard in banking
The general difference between scope and limits in coverage
questionBank.exp: NDIC's specific ownership split -- 60% CBN and 40% MOFI -- is institution-specific detail about Nigeria's deposit insurer, distinct from the general theoretical concepts of implicit/explicit schemes, moral hazard, and scope/limits covered as universal design principles. See 'NDIC: Ownership and Structure' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A bank's equity and reserves, expressed as a percentage of its risk-adjusted assets, form a cushion that protects depositors and other creditors against potential losses. What is this measure called?
opts: The deposit assessment base figure
Capital adequacy ratio
Liquidity coverage ratio
The premium rate percentage
questionBank.exp: A capital adequacy ratio measures a financial institution's equity and reserves as a percentage of its risk-adjusted assets, serving as a cushion against potential losses for depositors and creditors. The assessment base is a plausible-sounding distractor since both are percentage-based financial measures, but the assessment base is the deposit figure premiums are calculated against, not a capital cushion. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A newly independent country is designing its deposit insurance system and must choose between minimizing moral hazard and maximizing depositor confidence, since both cannot be fully achieved simultaneously through coverage limits alone. Which approach best balances this tradeoff?
opts: Set blanket coverage with a flat-rate premium for all banks
Set limited, explicit coverage with a differential premium system
Set implicit coverage with no defined limit at all
Set unlimited coverage funded by direct government subvention
questionBank.exp: The manual's framework points toward limited, explicit coverage combined with a differential premium system as the way to balance these competing goals: limited coverage curbs moral hazard while explicit, codified protection still builds genuine depositor confidence, and risk-based premiums reinforce sound bank behavior. Blanket coverage with flat-rate premiums moves in the opposite direction on both fronts, maximizing confidence in the short term while doing little to control moral hazard. See 'Coverage: Scope & Limits' and 'Differential Premium Assessment Approach' in the manual.

questionBank.q: In what year was the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation established through decree?
questionBank.exp: NDIC was established through Decree No. 22 of 15 June 1988, though it did not begin actual operations until March 1989. 1986 marks the introduction of the Structural Adjustment Program that prompted the reform, and 1992 is the year the number of licensed banks peaked at 120 -- both real dates from the same history, easily confused with the establishment year itself. See 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: NDIC's creation traces back to a committee set up in 1983 by which body, which recommended establishing a Depositors Protection Fund?
opts: The Federal Ministry of Finance's leadership
The Central Bank of Nigeria's Board
The National Assembly's finance committee
The Nigerian Stock Exchange's governing council
questionBank.exp: The history of NDIC originates in a committee set up in 1983 by the Board of the Central Bank of Nigeria to examine the banking system, which recommended establishing a Depositors Protection Fund. The Federal Ministry of Finance later became a co-owner of NDIC through MOFI, which makes it a tempting but historically incorrect answer to this specific origin question. See 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: The number of licensed banks in Nigeria grew from 40 in 1986 to 120 in 1992. Which of the following is listed as a direct consequence of this rapid increase?
opts: A reduction in banking sector competition
Questionable individuals becoming bank owners and managers
A steady decrease in demand for new bank licenses
Improved geographic distribution of bank branches
questionBank.exp: The rapid growth in licensed banks is explicitly linked to people of questionable integrity becoming bank owners and managers, alongside increased competition leading to sharp practices and inadequate manpower. A reduction in competition is the opposite of what actually happened, since more licensed banks increased competitive pressure rather than reducing it. See 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: In NDIC's early years, about how many distressed banks had Holding Actions imposed on them to restrict operations and encourage self-restructuring?
questionBank.exp: About 52 distressed banks had Holding Actions imposed on them in NDIC's early distress-management efforts. The other figures are real but describe different measures from the same period: 24 banks had their management taken over between 1991 and 1996, and 7 distressed banks were later restructured and handed to new investors in 1999-2000. See 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What was the primary purpose of the Failed Banks Decree No. 18 of 1994?
opts: To merge all distressed banks into a single national bank
To help distressed banks recover classified assets and punish contributing malpractices
To transfer bank supervision from NDIC to the CBN
To eliminate premium payments for well-managed banks
questionBank.exp: The Failed Banks Decree No. 18 of 1994 was intended to assist distressed banks in recovering their classified assets and to punish the malpractices that contributed to the distress, recovering about 3.3 billion naira by June 1996. Merging all distressed banks into one institution is a plausible-sounding but fictional response; the decree focused on asset recovery and accountability, not consolidation. See 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What is NDIC's stated Vision?
opts: To become the sole regulator of Nigeria's financial sector
To become a leading deposit insurer worldwide
To eliminate all bank failures in Nigeria
To provide unlimited deposit coverage to all Nigerians
questionBank.exp: NDIC's stated Vision is to become one of the leading deposit insurers in the world, a broad aspirational statement distinct from its Mission, which lists the specific means of protecting depositors. Becoming the sole financial regulator overstates NDIC's actual role, since supervision is shared and collaborative with the CBN rather than exclusive to NDIC. See 'NDIC - Vision & Mission' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as one of the four elements of NDIC's Mission statement?
opts: Direct management of all Nigerian commercial banks
Orderly resolution of failed insured financial institutions
Setting national interest rate policy
Issuing new bank licenses to qualified applicants
questionBank.exp: Orderly resolution of failed insured financial institutions is one of the four elements of NDIC's Mission, alongside effective supervision, financial/technical assistance, and prompt payment of guaranteed sums. Issuing bank licenses is actually a CBN function, not an NDIC one, making it a plausible-sounding but misattributed responsibility. See 'NDIC - Vision & Mission' in the manual.

questionBank.q: NDIC's mandate includes deposit guarantee, banking supervision, failure resolution, and bank liquidation -- a broad set of comprehensive risk-management functions. Which type of deposit insurer mandate does this combination represent?
opts: A pay-box mandate
A risk minimizer mandate
A pay-box plus mandate
A least-cost mandate
questionBank.exp: NDIC's combination of deposit guarantee, supervision, failure resolution, and liquidation powers is explicitly described as a risk minimizer mandate -- the broadest category on the mandate spectrum.
