NDIC's own establishment happened decades earlier, in 1988, well before either of these two reforms. See 'Recap: History of NDIC at a Glance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does the '2006' entry on Nigeria's banking history timeline specifically refer to?
opts: The founding of AMCON
The NDIC Act of 2006
The Banking Reform introducing the universal banking model
The Failed Banks Decree
questionBank.exp: The 2006 entry on the manual's timeline refers to the NDIC Act of 2006, which updated NDIC's original 1988 establishing decree. AMCON was founded later, in 2009, while the Failed Banks Decree dates to 1994, both distinct events from this specific 2006 legislative update. See 'Recap: History of NDIC at a Glance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Out of 25 local banks during an early period of banking distress, how many were ultimately liquidated?
questionBank.exp: The manual's timeline states that 21 of 25 local banks were liquidated during this early period, alongside a broader figure of 17 banks failing. Selecting 25 would claim every single local bank was liquidated, overstating what the timeline actually reports for this specific early distress period. See 'Recap: History of NDIC at a Glance' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A deposit insurer extends coverage to a pooled trust account by insuring each individual contributor's balance within that pool, rather than the pool as one lump sum. What is this arrangement called?
opts: Blanket coverage
Pass-through Insurance
Differential premium assessment
Open Bank Assistance
questionBank.exp: Pass-through Insurance (PTI) is exactly this arrangement: rather than insuring a pool or trust account up to the maximum as one unit, the balance of each individual contributor within that pool is insured separately. Blanket coverage instead means extending full protection to all depositors and creditors during a systemic crisis, an entirely different mechanism from insuring individual shares of a pooled account. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 6, in the manual.

questionBank.q: A subscriber holds funds through a mobile payment system whose accounts are structured as pooled deposits at a licensed institution. Under NDIC's pass-through insurance concept, is that individual subscriber entitled to deposit insurance coverage?
opts: No, coverage applies to the mobile payment operator, not subscribers
Yes, each mobile account holder is entitled to coverage
No, mobile money balances are excluded from deposit insurance coverage
Yes, but at half the standard insured limit
questionBank.exp: Yes -- through the pass-through insurance platform, each mobile money account holder is entitled to deposit insurance coverage as provided for in the enabling Act, since the underlying pooled account's contributors are individually insured rather than the pool as a whole. Claiming mobile money balances are entirely excluded from coverage contradicts this specific pass-through arrangement the manual describes NDIC extending to mobile payment subscribers. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 7, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the financial institutions NOT covered by NDIC's deposit insurance?
opts: Licensed commercial banks in Nigeria
The Bank of Industry
Non-Interest Banks nationwide
Microfinance Banks under NDIC
questionBank.exp: Development Finance Institutions such as the Bank of Industry, the Federal Mortgage Bank, the Bank of Agriculture, and the Infrastructure Bank are explicitly listed as institutions NOT covered by NDIC. Commercial banks, Non-Interest Banks, and Microfinance Banks are all instead explicitly listed among the institutions NDIC's deposit insurance does cover. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 8, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Besides Development Finance Institutions, which of the following is also listed among institutions NOT covered by NDIC?
opts: Primary Mortgage Institutions
Discount houses
Deposit Money Banks
Licensed merchant banks
questionBank.exp: Discount houses, along with finance companies, investment firms, unit trusts/mutual funds, insurance companies, and Pension Fund Administrators, are all listed among institutions NOT covered by NDIC. Primary Mortgage Institutions, by contrast, are explicitly among the institutions NDIC's insurance does cover, making this a natural but incorrect pairing. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 8, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Beyond Development Finance Institutions and discount houses, which of the following is also listed among institutions NOT covered by NDIC?
opts: Non-Interest Deposit-Taking Financial Institutions
Pension Fund Administrators
Deposit Money Banks
Primary Mortgage Banks
questionBank.exp: Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs), along with insurance companies, unit trusts, investment firms, finance companies, discount houses, and Development Finance Institutions, are all explicitly listed as NOT covered by NDIC. Non-Interest Deposit-Taking Financial Institutions are instead specifically named among the insured institutions, making them the natural but incorrect opposite answer here. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 8, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the deposits and instruments NOT insured by NDIC?
opts: Current account deposits
Inter-bank placements
Savings account deposits
Foreign currency deposits
questionBank.exp: Inter-bank placements, along with insider deposits, deposits held as collateral for loans, and investments such as stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and Treasury instruments, are listed among the deposits NOT insured by NDIC. Current account, savings account, and foreign currency deposits are all instead explicitly listed as insured deposit types. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 9, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an uninsured instrument, excluded from NDIC's deposit insurance coverage?
opts: Time or term deposits
Investment in mutual funds
Joint savings accounts held locally
Current account deposits nationwide
questionBank.exp: Investments such as stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities, commercial papers, and debentures are explicitly listed as uninsured instruments, distinct from the actual insured deposit types like current, savings, time, and joint accounts. Time or term deposits, by contrast, are specifically listed as insured, making this the natural but incorrect opposite answer. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 9, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as excluded from NDIC's deposit insurance coverage?
opts: Savings account deposits held locally
Treasury Bills, Bonds, and Notes
Foreign currency deposits held locally
Joint account deposits held locally
questionBank.exp: Federal Government Treasury Bills, Bonds, and Notes are listed as uninsured instruments, since they are government securities rather than bank deposits, even though NDIC itself invests the deposit insurance fund in similar instruments. Savings, foreign currency, and joint account deposits are all instead explicitly listed as insured deposit types under NDIC's coverage. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 9, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Whose bank deposits does NDIC insure, regardless of nationality?
opts: Deposits belonging to Nigerian citizens specifically
Deposits of natural and legal persons
Deposits belonging to registered companies specifically
Deposits belonging to government agencies specifically
questionBank.exp: NDIC insures bank deposits of natural persons as well as legal entities, no matter whether they are from Nigeria or from any other country -- coverage is not restricted by nationality or type of depositor. Restricting coverage to Nigerian citizens alone contradicts this explicit statement that foreign depositors are covered on the same basis as Nigerians. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 10, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which section of the NDIC Act 2006 gives NDIC the power to adopt any premium assessment system reflecting developments in the industry and economy?
opts: Section 17
Section 16(2)
Section 3
Section 22
questionBank.exp: Section 16(2) of the NDIC Act 2006 gives NDIC the power to adopt any premium assessment system to reflect developments in the industry and the economy generally, which is how the Differential Premium Assessment System was adopted. Section 17 is a real, related provision, but it concerns the certified deposit liability statement banks must submit as the assessment base, not the power to choose the assessment system itself. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 11, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How does NDIC protect the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF)?
opts: By keeping the entire fund as physical cash in a secure vault
By investing in safe, liquid instruments like Treasury Bills
By investing the fund directly in insured banks' shares
By distributing the fund evenly among all licensed banks
questionBank.exp: NDIC protects the Deposit Insurance Fund by investing it in safe but liquid financial instruments such as Treasury Bills, Federal Government Bonds, and instruments of a similar nature. Investing directly in insured banks' shares would actually be inappropriate, since the manual separately notes that shares are not considered safe for the deposit insurance fund. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 12, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Does NDIC finance its overhead and administrative expenses from the Deposit Insurance Fund itself?
opts: Yes, it draws directly from the DIF for all operating costs
No, it finances its expenses from its investment income
Yes, after depositors have been reimbursed each year
No, it relies mainly on annual government subvention
questionBank.exp: No -- NDIC finances all its overhead and administrative expenses from its investment income, mainly the proceeds from investing the DIF in Federal Government securities, and does not enjoy subvention from the government at all. Claiming it relies mainly on annual government subvention directly contradicts this explicit statement that NDIC receives no government subvention whatsoever. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 13, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Does NDIC's supervisory role duplicate the Central Bank of Nigeria's own bank supervision function?
opts: Yes, both institutions independently examine every bank every year with no coordination
No, the two institutions collaborate rather than duplicate efforts
Yes, NDIC's supervision has fully replaced the CBN's own supervisory role
No, because NDIC has no supervisory role of its own at all
questionBank.exp: No -- there is no duplication of supervisory functions; instead the NDIC and CBN collaborate through a joint committee on supervision and share banks for examination purposes, exchanging examination reports and sometimes conducting examinations jointly. Claiming NDIC's supervision has fully replaced the CBN's own role overstates the relationship, which the manual describes as collaborative, with both institutions retaining active supervisory involvement. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 14, in the manual.

questionBank.q: NDIC protects bank depositors against loss through deposit guarantee, failure resolution, and which third mechanism?
opts: Direct cash grants to every depositor
Bank supervision
Mandatory annual bank mergers
Unlimited blanket coverage at all times
questionBank.exp: The manual's Q&A section states NDIC protects bank depositors against loss through deposit guarantee, bank supervision (which reduces the potential risk of failure), and failure resolution (including financial and technical assistance to failing banks). Claiming NDIC provides unlimited blanket coverage at all times directly contradicts the manual's repeated emphasis that limited coverage, not blanket or unlimited protection, is best practice. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 15, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Under one payment method NDIC uses, it transfers an amount to another financial institution with instructions to pay depositors on its behalf. What is this method called?
opts: Direct cheque issuance
Deposit transfer
Purchase and Assumption
Open Bank Assistance
questionBank.exp: Deposit transfer involves NDIC transferring an amount equivalent to the total insured deposits to another financial institution, which then pays depositors on NDIC's behalf. Purchase and Assumption is a related but distinct method, where a healthy bank assumes deposit liabilities directly as part of a broader asset-and-liability transaction, not simply as a payment conduit. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 18, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Besides deposit transfer and Purchase and Assumption, what is a third method NDIC can use to pay depositors of a failed institution?
opts: Wiring funds directly to a random NDIC-selected bank
Issuing cheques collected at designated centers
Crediting a new mobile wallet for each depositor
Mailing physical cash to each depositor's home address
questionBank.exp: NDIC can pay depositors directly by issuing cheques up to the insured limit, which depositors collect at designated centers, usually the closed bank's own offices. Mailing physical cash to each depositor's home address is not among the listed payment methods, which focus on transfer, cheque issuance, and Purchase and Assumption instead. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 18, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How can Purchase and Assumption itself function as a method of paying insured depositors?
opts: NDIC issues each depositor a personal loan instead of a payout
A healthy bank assumes the failed bank's deposit liabilities
The failed bank's shareholders personally repay each depositor
The CBN prints new currency specifically to cover the shortfall
questionBank.exp: Payments could be made through Purchase and Assumption, where a healthy bank assumes part or all of the deposit liabilities of a failed insured bank, effectively paying depositors by taking over their accounts. Printing new currency to cover a shortfall is an extreme and unrelated response, nothing like the structured, bank-to-bank transaction the manual actually describes for P&A payments. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 18, in the manual.

questionBank.q: What specifically does a deposit transfer involve, as distinct from a direct cheque payment?
opts: NDIC personally visits each depositor's home to deliver funds
NDIC transfers the insured amount to another institution for depositor collection
NDIC converts insured deposits into shares of the assuming bank
NDIC cancels the insured deposits and issues new ones at a different bank
questionBank.exp: A deposit transfer involves NDIC transferring an amount equivalent to the total insured deposits of a failed institution to another financial institution under an agreement that lets depositors collect their entitlements from that institution. Converting insured deposits into shares of the assuming bank misrepresents the mechanism, which preserves the depositor's cash entitlement rather than converting it into equity. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 19, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Does NDIC's primary mandate directly protect the interests of a failed bank's creditors and shareholders?
opts: Yes, creditors and shareholders are NDIC's primary protected group
Not directly, but supervision indirectly protects them too
No, creditors and shareholders receive no consideration at all
Yes, but shareholders alone receive protection, never creditors
questionBank.exp: NDIC's primary mandate is to protect depositors, but through supervision that promotes safety and soundness, the interests of creditors and shareholders are also indirectly protected, and both can be paid liquidation dividends after depositors are fully reimbursed. Claiming creditors and shareholders receive no consideration at all contradicts this stated possibility of liquidation dividend payments to both groups. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 20, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How is a 'liquidation dividend' specifically defined?
opts: The annual profit NDIC distributes to the CBN and MOFI
Payment to a depositor of a failed institution beyond the insured sum
The interest rate NDIC pays on its Treasury Bill investments
The premium refund issued to well-managed banks each year
questionBank.exp: A liquidation dividend is defined as payment made to a depositor of a failed insured institution above the insured sum, funded from proceeds of asset sales and debt recoveries, distinct from the insured sum itself, which is paid from the DIF, SIIF, or NIDIF. An annual profit distribution to the CBN and MOFI is an unrelated concept, since NDIC's shareholders don't receive dividends from failed-bank liquidation proceeds. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 21, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Why must the insured limit be a definite, capped amount rather than unlimited?
opts: NDIC lacks the legal authority to set any limit at all
Unlimited coverage could create a perverse incentive for excessive risk-taking
The CBN prohibits deposit insurers from operating without a cap
Unlimited coverage would violate international banking treaties
questionBank.exp: The amount to be reimbursed must be definite, and limited coverage is designed specifically to minimize moral hazard through excessive risk-taking by bank management and depositors -- unlimited coverage could constitute a perverse incentive for exactly this kind of behavior. Claiming NDIC lacks legal authority to set any limit misrepresents the situation, since NDIC's Board explicitly has the power to set and review the limit. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 22, in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor has an account at a failed bank's main office and a separate account at one of its branches. How are these two accounts treated for insurance purposes?
opts: Insured completely separately, doubling the depositor's total coverage
Added together, since branches count as one institution
The main office account alone is eligible for coverage
The branch account alone is eligible for coverage
questionBank.exp: The main office and all branches of a bank are considered as one institution, so accounts held at different branches -- or at the main office and a branch -- are added together and insured up to the maximum insured sum as a single combined claim. Treating them as fully separate, doubled coverage is exactly the loophole this aggregation rule exists to prevent. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 23, in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor holds accounts at two different insured banks. Are the balances at these two banks added together to determine total insurance coverage?
opts: Yes, all balances across every bank are combined into one claim
No, each bank's deposits are insured independently up to the maximum limit
Yes, when both banks share the same parent holding company
No, because just one of the two banks can be insured at a time
questionBank.exp: The maximum insurance limit applies separately to deposits in each participating bank, so a depositor's balances at two different banks are insured independently, each up to the maximum insured sum. Combining all balances across every bank into a single claim would effectively force depositors below the true protection level the per-bank limit is meant to provide. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 24, in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor splits their funds into a current account and a savings account, both at the same bank and in the same right and capacity, hoping to double their insurance coverage. Does this strategy work?
opts: Yes, each different account type receives its own separate insured limit
No, same-capacity deposits are added together regardless of type
Yes, for accounts opened more than a year apart
No, because splitting funds across account types is against the law
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance is not increased merely by dividing funds held in the same right and capacity among different types of deposits -- demand, time, and savings accounts held by the same depositor in the same capacity are added together and insured up to the maximum insured sum as one combined claim. Claiming this splitting strategy is illegal overstates the situation; it simply doesn't achieve the extra coverage the depositor might be hoping for. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 25, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How is 'Purchase and Assumption' concisely defined?
opts: Purchasing a failed bank's brand name for resale to a foreign investor
Purchasing assets and assuming liabilities through another healthy bank
Assuming a failed bank's staff pension obligations, without its deposits
Purchasing government bonds to recapitalize a failed bank directly
questionBank.exp: Purchase and Assumption (P&A) is defined as a failure resolution mechanism involving purchasing the assets of a failed bank and assuming its liabilities by another healthy insured bank, or banks. Assuming only pension obligations without the deposits themselves misses the core purpose of P&A, which is specifically about transferring deposit liabilities to protect depositors. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 26, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How is 'Open Bank Assistance' concisely defined?
opts: A brand-new bank replacing the failed institution under a different name
A failed institution continuing to operate under the same name
A failed institution immediately entering full liquidation proceedings
A failed institution's assets being auctioned to the highest bidder
questionBank.exp: Open Bank Assistance (OBA) is defined as a situation where a failed insured institution can continue to operate in the same name as a going concern, possibly involving a change in ownership and management, fresh capital injection, and reorganization. A brand-new bank replacing the institution under a different name describes the separate Bridge Bank option instead, not OBA's defining feature of continuity under the same name. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 27, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How is a 'bridge bank' concisely defined?
opts: A permanent government-owned bank that never gets sold to investors
A temporary bank acquiring a failed bank's assets and liabilities
A temporary fund used to pay uninsured depositors
A joint venture between two healthy banks merging permanently
questionBank.exp: A bridge bank is defined as a temporary bank established and operated, usually by the deposit insurer, to acquire the assets and assume the liabilities of a failed bank until a final resolution is accomplished, permitting continuity of banking services. Describing it as a permanent government-owned bank contradicts its defining temporary nature -- it is specifically set up for a limited period while a buyer is found. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 28, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Why are the personal deposits of a bank's directors and staff excluded from deposit insurance coverage?
opts: Because directors and staff are legally prohibited from holding bank accounts
To create an incentive for them to manage the institution safely and soundly
Because their salaries are already fully insured under a separate scheme
Because they receive liquidation dividends instead of standard insurance
questionBank.exp: Directors' and staff deposits are excluded specifically to create an incentive for them to manage their institutions safely and soundly, reinforcing good corporate governance, since they would bear direct personal risk from mismanagement rather than being shielded by insurance. Claiming directors and staff are legally prohibited from holding bank accounts is a fabricated and implausible restriction not found anywhere in the manual. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 29, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Unlike directors' and staff deposits, why are a bank's shareholders' deposits still covered by deposit insurance?
opts: Because shareholders always hold larger deposit balances than staff
Because shareholders are not involved in the day-to-day running of the institution
Because shareholders pay a separate, additional insurance premium
Because shareholders are legally classified as depositors of a different bank
questionBank.exp: Shareholders' deposits remain covered because, unlike directors and staff, shareholders are not involved in the day-to-day running of their institutions, so excluding their deposits would not serve the same governance-incentive purpose. Claiming shareholders pay a separate additional premium for coverage is not something the manual describes; ordinary depositors, including shareholders, receive coverage automatically at no charge. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 29, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How does the purpose of deposit insurance differ from that of conventional property or life insurance?
opts: Deposit insurance is optional for insurers, while conventional insurance is always compulsory
Deposit insurance serves public welfare, while conventional insurance is commercial
Deposit insurance covers physical assets, while conventional insurance covers cash
Deposit insurance is regulated internationally, while conventional insurance is domestic
questionBank.exp: The purpose of deposit insurance is to protect depositors' rights, maintain credit order, and promote sound financial industry development, serving public welfare with no profit-earning motive, in contrast to conventional insurance companies, which are commercial enterprises. Claiming deposit insurance is optional for insurers reverses the actual best practice, since compulsory participation, not voluntary insurer choice, is the recommended approach. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How does the beneficiary structure of deposit insurance differ from that of conventional insurance?
opts: In deposit insurance, the insured party can freely designate any beneficiary it chooses
In deposit insurance, the insured institution and the beneficiary (depositors) are different parties
In deposit insurance, the government is the sole possible beneficiary
In deposit insurance, the beneficiary is typically a foreign entity
questionBank.exp: In deposit insurance, insured institutions pay premiums to NDIC, which reimburses the depositors of failed institutions if needed -- meaning the insured institution and the beneficiary (the depositors) are different parties. With conventional insurance, by contrast, the insured party can designate itself or another party as beneficiary, and can even be the beneficiary itself, a flexibility deposit insurance's beneficiary structure does not share. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How do the functions of deposit insurance differ from those of conventional insurance in terms of preventing losses?
opts: Deposit insurance pays claims strictly after an incident, exactly like conventional insurance
Deposit insurance actively works to prevent incidents, unlike conventional insurance
Deposit insurance has no claims process at all, unlike conventional insurance
Deposit insurance covers incidents retroactively for up to ten years
questionBank.exp: While both deposit insurance and conventional insurance pay claims after an incident occurs, the deposit insurance system in Nigeria takes active measures -- such as the Early-Warning System and off-site monitoring -- to help troubled institutions return to sound operations before an insurance incident is even deemed to have taken place. Claiming deposit insurance functions exactly like conventional insurance with no preventive role ignores this explicitly active, preventive dimension the manual describes. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How does the broader policy role of deposit insurance differ from that of conventional insurance?
opts: Deposit insurance sets national tax policy for the financial sector
Deposit insurance helps withdraw problem institutions to prevent systemic risk
Deposit insurance determines which companies may list on the stock exchange
Deposit insurance negotiates international trade agreements
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance plays a policy role as part of the financial safety net, helping the government establish mechanisms for withdrawing problem financial institutions from the market to effectively prevent systemic risk -- a public-policy function conventional insurance simply does not have. Setting national tax policy is an unrelated government function entirely outside deposit insurance's actual policy role as described in the manual. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How do participation conditions in deposit insurance differ from those in conventional insurance?
opts: Both deposit insurance and conventional insurance are typically voluntary
Deposit insurance participation is compulsory; conventional insurance is voluntary
Both deposit insurance and conventional insurance are typically compulsory
Deposit insurance is voluntary, while conventional insurance is typically compulsory
questionBank.exp: Best practice dictates that participation in deposit insurance should be compulsory, whereas participation in a conventional insurance contract is generally voluntary -- a direct contrast between the two systems' participation conditions. Reversing this, by claiming deposit insurance is voluntary while conventional insurance is compulsory, gets the actual recommended relationship backwards. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: How do typical coverage levels in deposit insurance differ from those in conventional insurance?
opts: Deposit insurance coverage is typically full, while conventional insurance is limited
Deposit insurance coverage is limited; conventional insurance may be full
Both deposit insurance and conventional insurance typically provide full coverage
Neither deposit insurance nor conventional insurance provides full coverage
questionBank.exp: Under deposit insurance, best practice prescribes that the amount of coverage should be limited, whereas conventional insurance coverage may be full -- a clear contrast in how much protection each system typically offers. Reversing this, by claiming deposit insurance coverage is typically full while conventional insurance is limited, gets the actual recommended relationship backwards. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 30, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Non-Interest Banking operates on Islamic principles that prohibit which specific practice in exchange contracts?
opts: Gharar, or speculative uncertainty
Riba, or interest
Maysir, or gambling
Zakat, or charitable giving
questionBank.exp: Non-Interest Banking prohibits riba, meaning interest, in exchange contracts, one of three core Islamic commercial-law prohibitions alongside gharar (speculative uncertainty) and maysir (gambling). Gharar and maysir are real, related prohibitions under the same framework, but they concern speculative business transactions and games of chance respectively, not interest itself. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 32, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which Non-Interest Banking principle specifically prohibits uncertainty or speculative behavior in business transactions?
opts: Riba
Gharar
Maysir
Sukuk
questionBank.exp: Gharar is the principle prohibiting uncertainty or speculative behavior in business transactions under Non-Interest Banking, distinct from riba (interest prohibition) and maysir (gambling prohibition). Sukuk is a real Islamic finance term, but it refers to an Islamic bond-like instrument, not a prohibition principle like gharar. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 32, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which Non-Interest Banking principle specifically prohibits any form of gambling?
opts: Riba
Maysir
Gharar
Zakat
questionBank.exp: Maysir is the principle prohibiting any form of gambling under Non-Interest Banking's Islamic commercial-law framework, alongside riba (interest) and gharar (speculative uncertainty). Zakat is a real Islamic concept related to charitable giving, but it is not one of the three prohibitions the manual specifically names for Non-Interest Banking. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 32, in the manual.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an area Non-Interest Banking prohibits funding for?
opts: Agricultural equipment
Alcohol production
Educational institutions
Renewable energy projects
questionBank.exp: Non-Interest Banking prohibits funding unethical concerns such as alcohol or tobacco production, ammunition manufacturing, and adult entertainment institutions. Agricultural equipment, educational institutions, and renewable energy projects are not among the prohibited funding areas the manual lists, and would generally be considered acceptable financing activities under Non-Interest Banking principles. See 'Appendix 1 - NDIC Q&A', Question 32, in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does 'resolution' mean in the context of a failing bank?
opts: The annual budget approved by a bank's board
The disposal plan and process for a non-viable bank
The routine renewal of a bank's operating license
The marketing strategy for a bank's new products
questionBank.exp: Resolution is defined in the glossary as the disposal plan and process for a non-viable bank, encompassing the various options like OBA, P&A, bridge bank, and liquidation. A routine license renewal describes an entirely different, ordinary regulatory process that applies to viable, functioning banks, not the specific disposal process for a non-viable one. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: What is a 'resolution authority'?
opts: A private law firm hired to represent a failed bank's shareholders
A public authority responsible for resolving institutions in its jurisdiction
An international body that sets global interest rate benchmarks
A rating agency that scores a bank's creditworthiness
questionBank.exp: A resolution authority is defined as a public authority that, either alone or together with other authorities, is responsible for the resolution of financial institutions in its jurisdiction, including resolution planning functions. A private law firm representing shareholders is a private commercial actor, not the public authority the glossary specifically describes holding this statutory resolution responsibility. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: What is the term for the legal entity that undertakes the winding-down of a failed bank and the disposal of its assets?
opts: Resolution authority itself
Liquidator (or receiver)
The deposit insurer directly
The bridge bank entity
questionBank.exp: The glossary defines a liquidator, also called a receiver, as the legal entity that undertakes the winding-down of the failed bank and the disposal of its assets -- the specific actor carrying out liquidation. A resolution authority is a broader, related concept: the public authority responsible for resolution generally, which may appoint or oversee the liquidator rather than being the liquidator itself. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A failed bank's asset is sold through a price directly negotiated between NDIC and a single interested buyer, rather than through a competitive bidding process. What is this sale method called?
opts: Purchase and Assumption
Private Treaty
Open Bank Assistance
Differential Premium Assessment
questionBank.exp: A Private Treaty is defined as an agreement for the sale of an asset at a price negotiated directly between the vendor and purchaser or their agents, distinct from a competitive bid process. The manual notes Private Treaty is adopted as an unavoidable option when competitive bidding isn't practical, part of the broader asset-recovery process, not a failure resolution option like Purchase and Assumption. See the Glossary of Terms and 'Maximize Recovery of Assets' in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does 'insolvency' mean for a financial institution?
opts: A situation where a bank's profits exceed its projected annual target
A situation where liabilities exceed assets or debts go unpaid
A situation where a bank changes its registered corporate name
A situation where a bank opens a new branch in a rural area
questionBank.exp: Insolvency is defined as a situation where a financial institution can no longer meet its financial obligations when due, or the value of its assets is less than the total of its debts -- the core financial condition that can trigger failure resolution. A bank exceeding its profit target describes financial strength, essentially the opposite condition from the distress insolvency represents. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does 'intervention' mean in a bank supervision context?
opts: A shareholder's personal investment decision outside regulatory scope
Any regulatory action addressing concerns at a bank
A routine customer complaint about a bank's service quality
A bank's own internal marketing campaign
questionBank.exp: Intervention is defined broadly as any action, including formal corrective action, taken by supervisory authorities, resolution authorities, or the deposit insurer to address concerns that may arise with a financial institution -- a broad umbrella covering everything from early intervention to formal resolution. A shareholder's personal, unrelated investment decision falls entirely outside this regulatory and supervisory scope the glossary describes. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does a deposit insurance fund's 'target fund size' refer to?
opts: The exact dollar amount NDIC must hold in physical cash reserves
The ex-ante fund size needed to meet future obligations
The maximum salary NDIC can pay its senior executives
The minimum number of licensed banks NDIC must supervise
questionBank.exp: Target fund size refers to the size of the ex-ante deposit insurance fund, typically measured as a proportion of the assessment base such as total or insured deposits, sufficient to meet expected future obligations and cover operational costs. A fixed physical cash reserve requirement misrepresents the concept, since the fund is invested in securities like Treasury Bills rather than held purely as physical cash. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: What does 'financial inclusion,' a major goal shared by NDIC and the CBN, refer to?
opts: The percentage of a bank's board seats held by women
Access individuals and entities have to formal financial services
The number of foreign banks operating in a country
The total value of a country's stock market
questionBank.exp: Financial inclusion refers to the extent to which individuals and entities have access to and utilize formal financial services, with expanding inclusion described as a major goal of both NDIC and the CBN. Stock market value is a real economic indicator, but it measures something entirely different from the access-to-services concept financial inclusion specifically describes. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: How is a 'bank' broadly defined?
opts: Any company listed on the Nigerian Stock Exchange
An entity licensed to accept deposits from the public
Any government agency that handles public funds
Any institution that issues loans to individuals
questionBank.exp: The glossary defines a bank broadly as any entity that is licensed to accept deposits or repayable funds from the public -- a definition centered on deposit-taking rather than any other single activity. An institution that issues loans to individuals could describe many non-bank lenders that don't take public deposits at all, making it a plausible but incomplete definition of what makes an entity a 'bank' specifically. See the Glossary of Terms in the manual.

questionBank.q: A mid-sized bank has failed, and NDIC wants depositors to experience the least possible disruption, with banking services continuing almost seamlessly under a new corporate identity while a buyer is sought. Which resolution option best fits this specific goal?
opts: The deposit pay-out option
The bridge bank option
Debt write-down and equity conversion
A permanent blanket guarantee
questionBank.exp: The bridge bank option is specifically designed to let banking transactions continue seamlessly without any break, since the bridge bank assumes all assets and liabilities and operates as a going concern while a buyer is found -- exactly the least-disruption goal described. Deposit pay-out, by contrast, involves a formal winding-up process where depositors must actually be paid out and later open new accounts elsewhere, a much more disruptive experience than the bridge bank's seamless continuity. See 'The Bridge Bank Option' in the manual.

questionBank.q: NDIC guarantees deposits, supervises banks, resolves failures, and liquidates failed institutions -- covering the full spectrum from prevention through to final closure. Which single mandate type from the typology best captures this end-to-end scope?
opts: Pay box
Risk minimizer
Loss minimizer
Pass-through
questionBank.exp: This full spectrum -- from supervision and risk management through to failure resolution and liquidation -- is exactly what defines a risk minimizer mandate, the broadest category on the deposit insurer mandate spectrum and the one NDIC itself holds. A pay box mandate, at the opposite narrow end, would cover only the deposit guarantee piece, none of the supervisory or resolution functions described here. See 'NDIC - Mandate, Powers & Functions' and 'DIS Mandates' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A depositor holds ₦450,000 in a savings account and ₦300,000 in a current account, both in their own name at the same failed Deposit Money Bank. How much of this combined ₦750,000 total is covered by deposit insurance?
opts: The full ₦750,000, since both accounts are insurable deposit types
₦500,000, the maximum insured limit for a DMB depositor
₦450,000, the larger of the two accounts alone
₦375,000, half of the combined total
questionBank.exp: Because both accounts are held in the same right and capacity at the same bank, they are merged and treated as one account totaling 750,000 naira -- but the insured payout is capped at the 500,000 naira maximum for a DMB depositor, with the remaining 250,000 naira potentially recoverable later through liquidation dividends. Claiming the full 750,000 is insured ignores the hard cap the insured limit places on the guaranteed payout itself. See 'Coverage - Claim' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's pre-1988 approach to failing banks relied on ad hoc government interventions with no fixed rules. Which broad shift does NDIC's subsequent establishment, with its codified limits and procedures, represent?
opts: A shift from explicit to implicit deposit insurance
A shift from implicit to explicit deposit insurance
A shift from compulsory to voluntary bank membership
A shift from risk minimizer to pay box mandate
questionBank.exp: NDIC's establishment through a codified decree, with defined limits, funding, and procedures, represents precisely the shift from implicit to explicit deposit insurance the manual describes as one of the core reasons deposit insurance systems are created. The reversed shift, from explicit to implicit, describes the opposite direction of change from what NDIC's own establishment actually represents. See 'Reasons for Deposit Insurance' and 'NDIC History' in the manual.

questionBank.q: A distressed bank has some remaining viable operations, and regulators want to both protect depositors immediately and preserve the possibility of the bank eventually returning to private ownership under better management. Considering speed, depositor protection, and eventual re-privatization together, which resolution option best balances all three goals?
opts: Immediate deposit pay-out and permanent liquidation
The bridge bank option
An indefinite, open-ended blanket guarantee
Transferring the bank's license to the CBN permanently
questionBank.exp: The bridge bank option is specifically designed to balance these three goals: it protects depositors immediately by assuming all assets and liabilities so banking continues seamlessly, while giving regulators time to nurture the bank back to health before selling it to new investors -- fulfilling the eventual re-privatization goal too. Immediate liquidation achieves fast depositor protection but forecloses any path back to private ownership, since the bank ceases to exist as a going concern. See 'The Bridge Bank Option' in the manual.

questionBank.q: Across both general deposit insurance theory and NDIC's specific implementation in Nigeria, what is the consistent, unifying goal both bodies of material return to again and again?
opts: Maximizing shareholder returns for insured banks
Protecting depositors while maintaining public confidence
Minimizing the number of licensed banks in the country
Eliminating all government involvement in banking
questionBank.exp: From the general theory's emphasis on public confidence and depositor protection through to NDIC's specific mandate, mission, and every resolution mechanism it employs, the consistent thread is protecting depositors while maintaining public confidence in the financial system -- the foundation the manual returns to from its opening page through its closing conclusions. Maximizing shareholder returns is not deposit insurance's goal at all; shareholders are protected only indirectly, and only after depositors are made whole. See 'What is Deposit Insurance?' and 'NDIC - Conclusions' in the manual.
